    One sitting state senator has been unseated, another trails by three

    look at the closest contests of the September 1 primary.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(glue)

tmap_mode("view")
```

```{r}
# Municipality-level results for the six races inside three points, frozen from
# the ma-election-db AP snapshot taken 2026-09-03 10:54 UTC. The upstream feed
# mutates in place, so the numbers here are pinned to that moment.
results_raw <- read_csv("close_primaries_2026_09_03.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Ballot names as they appear in the state's candidate listings, mapped to the
# forms these candidates are commonly known by. Only the differences are listed;
# every other name passes through unchanged.
display_names <- tribble(
    ~candidate_name,             ~display_name,
    "William N. Brownsberger",   "Will Brownsberger",
    "John Barrett",              "John Barrett III",
    "Gabriel Boomer Amaral",     'Gabriel "Boomer" Amaral',
    "Michael F. Rush",           "Michael Rush",
    "Persis S. Yu",              "Persis Yu",
    "Edward M. Pacheco",         "Edward Pacheco",
    "Stephen J. Medeiros",       "Stephen Medeiros",
    "Lora L. Wondolowski",       "Lora Wondolowski",
    "Corinne Ellen Coryat",      "Corinne Coryat",
    "Andrew J. Fitch",           "Andrew Fitch"
)

office_short <- function(office) {
    if_else(office == "State Representative", "House", "Senate")
}

#' Surname only, for map legends where the full name will not fit.
#' Drops a generational suffix first so "John Barrett III" gives "Barrett".
last_name <- function(full_name) {
    full_name |>
        str_remove("\\s+(Jr\\.?|Sr\\.?|I{2,3}|IV)$") |>
        word(-1)
}

results <- results_raw |>
    left_join(display_names, by = "candidate_name") |>
    mutate(
        display_name = coalesce(display_name, candidate_name),
        label        = str_glue("{display_name} ({party_abbr}-{candidate_city_town})"),
        label_inc    = if_else(is_incumbent == 1, str_c(label, "*"), as.character(label))
    )

# One row per candidate per race, with the race total and each candidate's share.
race_cand <- results |>
    group_by(
        office, district, district_display, party, party_abbr,
        race_call_status, eevp,
        display_name, label, label_inc, candidate_city_town, is_incumbent
    ) |>
    summarize(votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(office, district, party) |>
    mutate(
        race_votes = sum(votes),
        pct        = votes / race_votes
    ) |>
    ungroup()

# One row per race: the top two candidates, the margin, and AP's call status.
race_summary <- race_cand |>
    arrange(office, district, party, desc(votes)) |>
    group_by(office, district, district_display, party, party_abbr,
             race_call_status, eevp) |>
    summarize(
        leader       = first(label_inc),
        leader_votes = first(votes),
        leader_pct   = first(pct),
        runner       = nth(label_inc, 2),
        runner_votes = nth(votes, 2),
        runner_pct   = nth(pct, 2),
        total_votes  = first(race_votes),
        .groups      = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
        margin_votes = leader_votes - runner_votes,
        margin_pts   = (leader_pct - runner_pct) * 100,
        # "&" rather than "and" purely to keep the summary table narrow enough
        # to fit without horizontal scrolling.
        # The party is already evident from the candidate designations, so it is
        # left off the race name here.
        race         = str_glue(
            "{str_replace_all(district_display, ' and ', ' & ')} ",
            "{office_short(office)}"
        )
    ) |>
    arrange(margin_pts)

# The feed stamps snapshots in UTC; report the date in Eastern time, since
# that is the day a Massachusetts reader counts it as.
snapshot_date <- as.Date(
    as.POSIXct(max(results_raw$snapshot_time), format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OS", tz = "UTC"),
    tz = "America/New_York"
)

# "%d" zero-pads, so build the day from the integer to get "September 3".
snapshot_time <- str_glue(
    "{format(snapshot_date, '%B')} {as.integer(format(snapshot_date, '%d'))}"
)
```

Massachusetts held its state primary on September 1. We will look at
six state legislative races that have a margin of less than three
percentage points, including the Suffolk and Middlesex State Senate
race where incumbent Will Brownsberger (D-Belmont) is behind by three
ballots out of more than 24,000 ballots cast.

The numbers in this post come from the Associated Press
municipality-level feed, snapshotted on **`r snapshot_time`**, with
expected vote between 98% and 99% in each race. None of these results
are official, no municipality has certified, and AP still lists three
of the six as too early to call.

## The six closest races

```{r}
#| column: page
#| tbl-cap: |
#|   *The six September 1 primaries decided by less than three points, closest
#|   first. Vote shares are of the two-candidate total. An asterisk marks the
#|   incumbent.*

race_summary |>
    mutate(
        leader_disp = str_glue(
            "{format(leader_votes, big.mark = ',')} ",
            "({sprintf('%.1f', leader_pct * 100)}%)"
        ),
        runner_disp = str_glue(
            "{format(runner_votes, big.mark = ',')} ",
            "({sprintf('%.1f', runner_pct * 100)}%)"
        ),
        status = if_else(race_call_status == "Called", "Called", "Too early")
    ) |>
    select(race, leader, leader_disp, runner, runner_disp,
           margin_votes, margin_pts, status) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(
        race         = "Race",
        leader       = "Leading",
        leader_disp  = "Votes",
        runner       = "Trailing",
        runner_disp  = "Votes",
        margin_votes = "Margin",
        margin_pts   = "Pts",
        status       = "AP"
    ) |>
    fmt_number(margin_votes, decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_number(margin_pts, decimals = 2) |>
    cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(leader_disp, runner_disp)) |>
    tab_style(
        style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
        locations = cells_body(columns = c(margin_votes, margin_pts))
    ) |>
    tab_source_note(md(glue(
        "*\\* Incumbent. Source: Associated Press municipality-level returns, ",
        "snapshot of {snapshot_time}.*"
    ))) |>
    tab_options(
        table.font.size = px(12),
        table.width = pct(100)
    )
```

Three of the six close legislative primaries were challenges to an
incumbent.  Senator Will Brownsberger (D-Belmont) is down by 3 votes
in a race that is too close to call, Senator Michael Rush (D-Boston)'s
challenger Persis Yu (D-Boston) has been declared the winner, and
Representative John Barrett (D-North Adams) has been declared the
winner by 159 votes.

```{r}
# Precinct geometry and the precinct-to-district mapping, both from mapoli.
prec_geom <- read_sf(paste0(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/",
    "gis/geojson/wardsprecincts2022.geojson"
))

city_town_geom <- read_sf(paste0(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/",
    "gis/geojson/city_town_2024.geojson"
)) |>
    select(city_town, geometry) |>
    st_make_valid()

prec_dist <- read_csv(
    paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/",
           "pvi/ma_precincts_districts_pres_2024.csv"),
    show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
    select(city_town, ward, precinct, State_Rep, State_Senate)

#' Town-level geometry for a district.
#'
#' A municipality wholly inside the district gets its full municipal boundary;
#' one split between districts gets only its in-district precincts, dissolved.
#' The whole-town path matters because a handful of precincts split by the 2021
#' redistricting (Walpole 2A and 5A, for instance) carry ward/precinct codes
#' that the 2022 precinct shapefile does not have.
district_towns <- function(office_name, district_name) {
    dist_col <- if (office_name == "State Representative") "State_Rep" else "State_Senate"

    in_dist <- prec_dist |>
        filter(.data[[dist_col]] == district_name)

    town_split <- in_dist |>
        count(city_town, name = "n_in_district") |>
        left_join(
            prec_dist |>
                filter(city_town %in% in_dist$city_town) |>
                count(city_town, name = "n_total"),
            by = "city_town"
        ) |>
        mutate(is_split = n_in_district < n_total)

    whole_geom <- city_town_geom |>
        filter(city_town %in% town_split$city_town[!town_split$is_split])

    split_towns <- town_split$city_town[town_split$is_split]

    split_geom <- in_dist |>
        filter(city_town %in% split_towns) |>
        inner_join(prec_geom, by = c("city_town", "ward", "precinct")) |>
        st_as_sf() |>
        st_make_valid() |>
        group_by(city_town) |>
        summarize(.groups = "drop") |>
        st_make_valid() |>
        st_buffer(dist = 10) |>
        st_buffer(dist = -10)

    bind_rows(whole_geom, split_geom) |>
        st_make_valid() |>
        st_simplify(dTolerance = 25)
}

#' Town-level two-candidate results for one race, in wide form.
race_towns <- function(office_name, district_name, party_name) {
    ord <- race_cand |>
        filter(office == office_name, district == district_name, party == party_name) |>
        arrange(desc(votes))

    lead_name <- ord$display_name[1]
    run_name  <- ord$display_name[2]

    results |>
        filter(office == office_name, district == district_name, party == party_name) |>
        select(city_town, display_name, votes) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = display_name, values_from = votes, values_fill = 0) |>
        mutate(
            lead_votes = .data[[lead_name]],
            run_votes  = .data[[run_name]],
            total      = lead_votes + run_votes,
            lead_pct   = lead_votes / total,
            run_pct    = run_votes / total,
            margin     = (lead_pct - run_pct) * 100,
            margin_clamped = pmax(pmin(margin, 40), -40)
        ) |>
        select(city_town, lead_votes, run_votes, total, lead_pct, run_pct,
               margin, margin_clamped) |>
        arrange(desc(total))
}

# Purple-green diverging scale: green towns went to the race leader, purple to
# the trailing candidate. Deliberately not red/blue -- five of these six races
# are contests between two candidates of the same party.
margin_palette <- c(
    "#762A83", "#9970AB", "#C2A5CF", "#E7D4E8", "#F7F7F7",
    "#D9F0D3", "#A6DBA0", "#5AAE61", "#1B7837"
)

#' Interactive town map for one race, filled by two-candidate margin.
race_map <- function(office_name, district_name, party_name) {
    ord <- race_cand |>
        filter(office == office_name, district == district_name, party == party_name) |>
        arrange(desc(votes))

    lead_name <- ord$display_name[1]
    run_name  <- ord$display_name[2]

    town_results <- race_towns(office_name, district_name, party_name) |>
        mutate(
            lead_disp   = str_glue("{lead_votes} ({sprintf('%.1f', lead_pct * 100)}%)"),
            run_disp    = str_glue("{run_votes} ({sprintf('%.1f', run_pct * 100)}%)"),
            margin_disp = str_glue(
                "{if_else(margin >= 0, lead_name, run_name)} ",
                "+{sprintf('%.1f', abs(margin))}"
            )
        )

    town_geom <- district_towns(office_name, district_name) |>
        left_join(town_results, by = "city_town")

    town_centroids <- town_geom |>
        st_centroid() |>
        select(city_town, geometry)

    popup_vars <- c("City/Town" = "city_town")
    popup_vars[lead_name]  <- "lead_disp"
    popup_vars[run_name]   <- "run_disp"
    popup_vars["Margin"]   <- "margin_disp"
    popup_vars["Total"]    <- "total"

    (tm_shape(town_geom) +
        tm_polygons(
            fill       = "margin_clamped",
            fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
                values   = margin_palette,
                limits   = c(-40, 40),
                midpoint = 0,
                ticks    = c(-40, -20, 0, 20, 40),
                # Negative is the trailing candidate's end of the scale, so the
                # surnames sit at their own extremes and name the two colors.
                labels   = c(
                    str_glue("{last_name(run_name)} 40+"), "20", "even", "20",
                    str_glue("{last_name(lead_name)} 40+")
                )
            ),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Margin\n(points)"),
            fill_alpha  = 0.7,
            popup.vars  = popup_vars
        ) +
        tm_shape(town_centroids) +
        tm_text("city_town", size = 0.8) +
        tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap"))
}

#' Municipality vote table for one race, with a district total row.
race_table <- function(office_name, district_name, party_name) {
    ord <- race_cand |>
        filter(office == office_name, district == district_name, party == party_name) |>
        arrange(desc(votes))

    lead_name <- ord$display_name[1]
    run_name  <- ord$display_name[2]

    town_results <- race_towns(office_name, district_name, party_name)

    totals <- town_results |>
        summarize(
            city_town  = "District total",
            lead_votes = sum(lead_votes),
            run_votes  = sum(run_votes),
            total      = sum(total)
        ) |>
        mutate(
            lead_pct = lead_votes / total,
            run_pct  = run_votes / total,
            margin   = (lead_pct - run_pct) * 100
        )

    bind_rows(town_results |> select(-margin_clamped), totals) |>
        # Margin in votes as well as points: in races this close, the raw vote
        # gap in each municipality is what actually adds up to the result.
        mutate(margin_votes = lead_votes - run_votes) |>
        select(city_town, lead_votes, lead_pct, run_votes, run_pct,
               margin_votes, margin, total) |>
        gt() |>
        cols_label(
            city_town    = "City/Town",
            lead_votes   = "Votes",
            lead_pct     = "%",
            run_votes    = "Votes",
            run_pct      = "%",
            margin_votes = "Votes",
            margin       = "Pts",
            total        = "Total"
        ) |>
        tab_spanner(label = lead_name, columns = c(lead_votes, lead_pct)) |>
        tab_spanner(label = run_name, columns = c(run_votes, run_pct)) |>
        tab_spanner(label = "Margin", columns = c(margin_votes, margin)) |>
        fmt_number(c(lead_votes, run_votes, total), decimals = 0) |>
        fmt_percent(c(lead_pct, run_pct), decimals = 1) |>
        fmt_number(margin_votes, decimals = 0) |>
        fmt_number(margin, decimals = 1) |>
        tab_style(
            style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cell_fill(color = "#f0f0f0")),
            locations = cells_body(rows = city_town == "District total")
        ) |>
        tab_options(
            table.font.size = px(13),
            table.width = pct(100)
        )
}
```

## Suffolk and Middlesex Senate: 3 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Suffolk and Middlesex Senate Democratic primary. Click a municipality
#|   for its vote totals.*

race_map("State Senate", "Suffolk and Middlesex", "Democratic")
```

Will Brownsberger has represented this district since 2012 after
serving five years as a Representative in the House and chairs the
Senate's Judiciary Committee. Daniel Lander is a first-time candidate
from the Fenway neighborhood of Boston and is a former senior policy
adviser to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu. Lander ran against the Beacon
Hill status quo, but geographical affiliation seems to have played a
role as well, with Brownsberger's base in suburban Belmont, while
roughly half the district's votes are cast in Boston and Cambridge.

Brownsberger carried exactly one municipality—Belmont, where he
lives—but he carried it by 37.8 points, a 2,181-vote cushion out of
5,767 cast. Lander won everywhere else: Boston by 21 points, Cambridge
by 7, and Watertown, the district's second-largest vote center, by 175
votes—very close to a tie. AP's count as of this snapshot has Lander
ahead by three votes out of 24,261—a margin of one hundredth of a
percentage point.

The lead has moved more than once. The
[Watertown News](https://watertownmanews.com/2026/09/02/state-senate-race-heading-to-recount-brownsberger-holds-narrow-lead/)
and [Boston.com](https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2026/09/02/razor-thin-margin-separates-state-sen-brownsberger-and-former-wu-aide-lander-setting-up-possible-recount/)
have both described the race as headed for a recount. No Republican filed here, so the
recount decides the seat.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| tbl-cap: |
#|   *Suffolk and Middlesex Senate Democratic primary, by municipality.*

race_table("State Senate", "Suffolk and Middlesex", "Democratic")
```

## Ninth Bristol House: 14 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Ninth Bristol House Democratic primary.*

race_map("State Representative", "Ninth Bristol", "Democratic")
```

Eight-term Democrat Christopher Markey (D-Dartmouth) stepped down as
State Representative to run for Bristol County District Attorney and
will face Republican Seth Aitken (R-Swansea) in November. Two
Dartmouth Democrats—Edward Pacheco, a bartender and transit manager,
and Stephen Medeiros, who works in South Coast real estate—competed to
replace him. Both campaigned against three large proposed housing
developments that would push Dartmouth past the 10% affordable-housing
threshold in state law [New Bedford
Light](https://newbedfordlight.org/pacheco-inches-past-medeiros-in-democratic-primary-for-9th-bristol/).

The district consists of Dartmouth, which cast 4,142 of the 4,924
votes, and a small slice of New Bedford. Both municipalities were
nearly tied—Pacheco won Dartmouth by 22 votes, Medeiros took the New
Bedford precincts by 8—which is how a race ends up 14 votes
apart. This is one of only two of the six races where the winner will
be competing against a candidate from the other party in November, in
this case Republican Chester Tam of Dartmouth who won his party's
nomination unopposed.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| tbl-cap: |

race_table("State Representative", "Ninth Bristol", "Democratic")
```

## First Franklin House: 98 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *First Franklin House Democratic primary. This is the largest of the six
#|   districts—18 municipalities, most of them very small.*

race_map("State Representative", "First Franklin", "Democratic")
```

The First Franklin has been vacant since January, when Natalie Blais
resigned to take an administrative post at UMass Amherst. Lora
Wondolowski, president of the Greenfield City Council and founding
executive director of the Massachusetts League of Environmental
Voters, faced Corinne Coryat of Deerfield, who had been Blais's
legislative aide. Housing was the central issue of the campaign, and
both candidates were
[pressed on it](https://recorder.com/2026/08/26/wondolowski-coryat-housing-debate/)
in the closing weeks.

The eighteen towns of the district stretch from Montague and
Greenfield west to hill towns like Monroe, Hawley, and Rowe that cast
fewer than 100 votes each. Coryat carried 10 of the 18 municipalities,
including her own Deerfield by 17 points, but Wondolowski won the two
largest towns of Montague and Greenfield, which provided a third of
the district's votes, leading to an overall margin of 98
votes. Wondolowski will face independent Amy Lavallee (I-Whately) in
November.

```{r}

#| tbl-cap: |
#|   *First Franklin House Democratic primary, by municipality.*

race_table("State Representative", "First Franklin", "Democratic")
```

## First Bristol and Plymouth Senate: 84 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *First Bristol and Plymouth Senate Republican primary.*

race_map("State Senate", "First Bristol and Plymouth", "Republican")
```

This is the one Republican primary on the list. Gabriel "Boomer"
Amaral of Fall River—who came close to winning the Fall River
mayoralty in 2025—beat Manny Silva of Somerset, a teacher's aide and
retired IT specialist, for the right to challenge Senate Ways and Means
Chair Michael Rodrigues, the Westport Democrat who has held the seat
since 2011.

The map is a clean split between Amaral's city and Silva's suburbs.
Amaral took Fall River by 666 votes and added smaller wins in
Westport, Freetown, and a tiny three-vote edge in Lakeville. Silva won
everywhere else: Somerset by 322, Swansea by 224, and Rochester
by 186.

## Norfolk and Suffolk Senate: 653 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Norfolk and Suffolk Senate Democratic primary.*

race_map("State Senate", "Norfolk and Suffolk", "Democratic")
```

Michael Rush has held this senate seat since 2011, after serving eight
years in the House, and had not faced a primary or general
election opponent since 2012. Persis Yu, a Hyde Park attorney who has
spent her career litigating on behalf of student loan borrowers and
consumers—first at the National Consumer Law Center, then at Protect
Borrowers—ran against Rush and has been called as the winner by the
AP.

Yu dominated in the Boston neighborhoods of West Roxbury, Roslindale,
Hyde Park, and Jamaica Plain which provided over half of the primary
votes. Rush won in all of the surrounding municipalities of Dedham,
Norwood, Walpole, and Westwood. Rush declined Yu's [invitations to debate](https://www.electpersis.com/news/state-senate-challenger-calls-for-debate),
a decision that drew attention through a campaign in which he was
[largely absent from candidate forums](https://www.universalhub.com/2026/state-senator-had-tough-choice-yesterday-attend-forum-whose-date-he).
There is no Republican filer for the seat and Yu will likely be sworn
in as senator in January, 2027.


## First Berkshire House: 159 votes

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *First Berkshire House Democratic primary.*

race_map("State Representative", "First Berkshire", "Democratic")
```

Representative John Barrett (D-North Adams) is the one challenged
incumbent in this group who has been declared as the winner. Barrett
was mayor of North Adams for 26 years before winning this House seat
in a 2017 special election after the death of Rep. Gailanne Cariddi
(D-North Adams), and his career in Berkshire politics goes back
to 1984. Andrew Fitch (D-North Adams), vice president of the North
Adams City Council since 2023, ran his first campaign for state office
against him.

The two [agreed on most of the district's
problems](https://www.nepm.org/regional-news/2026-08-27/1st-berkshire-race-pits-incumbent-rep-against-north-adams-city-councilor)—the
regional economy, housing, an aging population—and differed mainly on
whether experience or a fresh perspective was the better answer.
Barrett ran on his record of steering state money to the northern
Berkshires. He won 11 of the district's 13
municipalities. Williamstown, home to Williams College, went to Fitch
by 20 points and 309 votes.  Barrett survived because he broke even in
the North Adams they share, winning it by 44 votes, and getting 
double-digit margins in Adams, Cheshire, Hinsdale, and the hill
towns. There will be no Republican on the ballot in November.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| tbl-cap: |
#|   *First Berkshire House Democratic primary, by municipality.*

race_table("State Representative", "First Berkshire", "Democratic")
```

## Possible recounts

Massachusetts allows a candidate to request a recount by petition, and
recounts are likely to be requested in the closest of these races.

*Results in this post come from the Associated Press municipality-level
feed as collected in
[ma-election-db](https://github.com/bwbensonjr/ma-election-db), snapshot
of `r snapshot_time`. District geography and precinct assignments come
from [mapoli](https://github.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli). The frozen data
file used here is
[`close_primaries_2026_09_03.csv`](close_primaries_2026_09_03.csv).*
